title: Undercut and Rally
teaches: The undercut and rally as we trade it: a leader dips a few cents to a few percent under a level everyone can see, then takes it back within three sessions. We buy with a market order as price trades back over the level, never the undercut itself. The stop sits a few cents under the undercut low, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, and a loss at the stop is the plan working.

walkthroughs.title: QCOM, September 2020: the same-day trap
steps: Two weeks of flat shelf on the 50-day. That's QCOM in September 2020, and the level is 109.62.
September 21 the low hits 108.30, 1.20% under. Same day it's back over 109.62. That's the trap.
Never buy the undercut. Buy at market as it clears the level, 109.63. Stop 108.25, under the undercut low.
A close back under 109.62 is the warning. It closes near the high instead, 3R the next day, then 37.3R.

walkthroughs.title: WYNN, November 2013: two closes under, then a gap back
steps: WYNN, November 2013. The level is 159.37, from November 7. It closes under it two days running.

Buy at market on the open, 159.97, only 0.4% over the level. Stop 157.43, under the undercut low, 1.59% away.
A trade under 157.43 is the exit. It held, but slow: 3R took 8 days. Then it ran to 26.0R.

questions.q: A leader everyone's watching breaks under a low that held for weeks. By the close it's back over it. What happened?
choices: It dipped under a level and took it back
It broke out over a flat ceiling
It drifted lower under its 200-day
It gapped up on a strong earnings report
questions.answer: It dipped under a level and took it back
questions.why: It dipped under a level and took it back. That's an undercut and rally, a U&R. The break of the low hits everybody's stops and pulls in the shorts. Then price trades right back over it, and they're all on the wrong side. That trap is the edge. A breakout, a gap up or a slow drift never breaks a level and takes it back.
questions.lesson_line: Breaks the level, takes it right back. That's the trap we buy.

choices: A close under the 9 EMA
A close under the 200-day
A new 5-day low close
A trade under the undercut low
questions.why: A close under the 9 EMA. On a fast mover, the 9 EMA rides right under the trend. As long as it closes above it, you let it run. A steadier stock gets the 20 EMA instead, so a normal pullback doesn't knock you out. Use the close, not a poke under the line during the day.
questions.lesson_line: Fast mover, 9 EMA. Steadier, 20 EMA. Sell on a close under.

wrong.A trade under the undercut low: That was your first stop. By now the trail does the work.
wrong.A close under the 200-day: Way too loose. You'd give back most of the move.
wrong.A new 5-day low close: That's not our trail. We trail with the 9 or the 20 EMA.

questions.simple: A close under the 9 EMA. Fast movers ride the 9, steadier names ride the 20.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (the default trail, adjustable)

questions.q: Ten sessions in and it's going nowhere. What's the move?
choices: Sell it and free up the money
Hold, the stop hasn't been hit
Sell part of it into strength
Move the stop to breakeven now
questions.answer: Sell it and free up the money
questions.why: Sell it. Ten trading days and still under 1R means it isn't doing what a U&R should. A good trap works fast. Meanwhile that money could be in something that's moving. So we sell and free the cash. The stop not being hit doesn't make it a good trade. It just makes it a slow one.
questions.lesson_line: Ten sessions, under 1R: out.

wrong.Sell part of it into strength: There's no strength to sell into. It's sitting at 0.4R.
wrong.Hold, the stop hasn't been hit: The stop isn't the only exit. Time is one too.
wrong.Move the stop to breakeven now: Breakeven comes after it's made 2R to 5R, or at your first sell. Neither happened.

questions.story: Ten sessions after the buy, the stock sits at 0.4R. The stop has not been hit and no trim has come off.
questions.simple: Sell it. Under 1R after ten trading days, the money works better somewhere else.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (the time stop)

questions.q: The first 30 minutes are done. What's the call?
choices: Get out of the whole position
Set the stop at 131.20 and hold
Keep the 133.69 stop and wait
Buy more at the lower price
questions.answer: Get out of the whole position
questions.why: Get out. On a gap through your stop, the low of the first 30 minutes becomes the new stop. But there's a ceiling. If that low puts the loss past 2R, you're done. Your 2R line is two times 1.69 under the 135.38 buy, and 131.20 sits below it. That ceiling keeps one bad gap from turning into a disaster.
questions.lesson_line: On a gap, the first 30 minutes decide. Past 2R, you're out.

wrong.Set the stop at 131.20 and hold: That would be the new stop, except it's past the 2R ceiling. Past 2R you're out.
wrong.Keep the 133.69 stop and wait: Price is already through it. The gap rule hands the stop to the first 30 minutes.
wrong.Buy more at the lower price: Never add to a loser that gapped through its stop.

questions.story: You bought at 135.38 with the stop at 133.69. Your 1R is 1.69. The next day gaps down to 131.90, and the first 30-minute low is 131.20.
questions.simple: Get out. The first 30-minute low puts the loss past 2R, and past 2R we're out.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (the gap rule and its 2R ceiling)
the key needs arithmetic on the story's numbers

questions.q: It gaps open over your 3R mark. What do you do with it?
choices: Selling some here is your call
Sell a third, it's past 3R
Wait for 113.77 on the way back
Sell the whole position at the open
questions.answer: Selling some here is your call
questions.why: Your call. A gap over 3R isn't an automatic sell. But look at what you have: a three-day push that just gapped higher. That's the kind of strength I like to sell some into. Selling a piece here is a fine choice, and so is holding with the trail. Either way, don't wait for 113.77 to come back. It may never.
questions.lesson_line: A gap past 3R isn't an automatic sell. Selling some is your call.

wrong.Sell the whole position at the open: Too much at once. Sell some if you like, and let the trail handle the rest.
wrong.Sell a third, it's past 3R: 3R is a mark, not a sell order. No gap forces a sale.
wrong.Wait for 113.77 on the way back: A strong stock may never come back to it. Decide on the gap you have.

questions.story: You bought at 109.63 with the stop at 108.25. Your 3R level is 113.77. The stock pushes up for three days, then opens at 115.20.
questions.simple: It's your call. Selling some into a gap after a push is fine, and holding is fine too.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (the gap-open trim)

questions.q: A stock trades 2 million shares a day. Owning 100,000 shares of it, 5% of that volume, is fine.
questions.why: False. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, so 100,000 is five times our limit. The reason is getting out. If it turns, you need buyers for your shares without crushing the price. Stay small against the volume and you can always leave. If a name's too thin for your size, it's not on the list.
questions.lesson_line: Stay under 1% of daily volume. You have to be able to get out.
questions.simple: False. We stay under 1% of daily volume, so we can always get out clean.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (the volume limit)

questions.q: You just sold some into a strong 5-day push. Where does the stop on the rest go?
choices: Up to breakeven, your entry
Back under the undercut low
Down a bit, to give it room
Leave it at the original stop
questions.why: Up to breakeven, your entry. Once you've sold some, the rest shouldn't turn into a loser. Moving the stop to your entry makes sure of that. We move it there somewhere between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell. From here the worst case on the rest is a scratch, and the trail takes over.
questions.lesson_line: Once you sell some, the stop on the rest goes to breakeven.

wrong.Back under the undercut low: That's where it started. After a sell you protect the rest.
wrong.Leave it at the original stop: Then a winner you already sold into can still turn into a full loss.

questions.simple: Up to your entry. After a sell, the rest of the trade shouldn't turn into a loss.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (breakeven timing)

questions.q: Pretty trap. Do you take it?
choices: Pass, the 50-day is falling
Take it, the reclaim proves it
Take it, the 20 EMA is rising
Wait for the 200-day to turn up
questions.why: Pass. The 50-day is lower than it was 10 sessions ago, so it's rolling over. I want this trap in a leader that's trending, not in a stock that's sliding. Under a falling 50-day, a quick reclaim can just be a bounce on the way down. That's normally a pass for me. A clean trap doesn't fix a broken trend.
questions.lesson_line: Check the 50-day before you trust the trap.

wrong.Wait for the 200-day to turn up: The problem here is the falling 50-day, not the 200-day.
wrong.Take it, the reclaim proves it: The reclaim is only half the check. The trend under it is falling.
wrong.Take it, the 20 EMA is rising: A short bounce can lift the 20 EMA. The 50-day is the trend, and it's falling.

questions.story: A quick undercut and a reclaim in two sessions. The 50-day is lower than it was 10 sessions ago.
questions.simple: Pass. A falling 50-day means the trend is down, and a trap doesn't fix that.

reasons: the 50-day check c09 is a proposed card line
both facts come from the same card

questions.q: Our market filter reads Orange, one step from Red. Your U&R grades a B. You can still take it.
questions.why: False. Orange is A+ only for us. When the market's under pressure, setups fail more because nothing's backing them. So I only want my very best idea, and a B isn't it. It can wait for a better market. Green is when we press. Red is mostly cash.
questions.lesson_line: Orange means A+ only. A B waits.
questions.simple: False. In Orange we only take A+ setups, because the market isn't backing anything less.

reasons: market reading levels are the owner's rule F65
fixed before

questions.q: Gorgeous chart, ugly market. What's the call?
choices: Skip it, stay mostly in cash
Take it, the setup is clean
Take it full size, it's a leader
Wait for a second reclaim day
questions.answer: Skip it, stay mostly in cash
questions.why: Skip it. Red means we're mostly in cash, and the index just broke down. A U&R needs the market behind it. When ours fail, it's mostly while the index is breaking down. ADBE looked fine in a weak market, got bought, and was stopped the next day. SPY made a lower low days later. Keep the name on your list for when the market turns.
questions.lesson_line: The market beats a pretty chart.

wrong.Wait for a second reclaim day: A second reclaim doesn't fix the market. Wait for the market to turn.
wrong.Take it, the setup is clean: A clean chart doesn't change the market. Failed U&Rs come as the index breaks down.
wrong.Take it full size, it's a leader: Full size is for a Green market. In Red we're mostly cash.

questions.story: A leader makes a textbook U&R of its 20 EMA. The index broke down yesterday. The market reading is Red.
questions.simple: Skip it. In a Red market we're mostly cash, and these traps fail when the index is falling.

reasons: market reading levels are the owner's rule F65
fixed before

questions.q: You're buying this reclaim of the 20 EMA. Where's your stop?
choices: Just under the undercut low
1% to 2% under the average
Under the 200-day average
Right at the average itself
questions.why: Just under the undercut low, which is the low of the day here. Same trap, same stop. Price already went under the 20 EMA once today, so a stop at the line gets hit by the same wiggle. The low of the dip is where the idea is wrong. Go a few cents under it and you're set.
questions.lesson_line: Same trap, same stop: under the undercut low.

wrong.Under the 200-day average: Way too far. That's not a stop, it's a hope.
wrong.Right at the average itself: It already went under the average today. The same wiggle stops you out.
wrong.1% to 2% under the average: Some traders do that. We keep the stop under the low of the dip, where the trade is actually wrong.

questions.simple: Under the undercut low, the low of the day here. That's where the trap is proven wrong.

reasons: the few-cents stop is the owner's rule F62
fixed before

questions.story: The reclaim day. Its low undercut the 20 EMA and the close took it back.

deeper.counter: Morales and Kacher let the moving average U&R stop sit 1-2% below the line. Ours goes under the undercut low on every U&R, so the same trap gets the same stop.

questions.q: IBD's shakeout-plus-three waits until price is three points over the first low. That's a later buy than ours.
questions.why: True. IBD's version has two lows, the second undercutting the first. Their buy point is three points over that first low. We buy the moment price trades back over the level, so we're in earlier and closer to the stop. Waiting for their proof gives up part of the move and widens the stop. Ours is tighter.
questions.lesson_line: IBD waits three points. We buy the reclaim.
questions.simple: True. They wait for three points of proof, and we buy the reclaim itself, earlier and closer to the stop.

reasons: the trigger style waits on D-003
the card's option C line is proposed

questions.q: Your U&R could trigger tomorrow. The level, your stop and your size should be written down before the open.
questions.why: True. Do the thinking at night, when nothing's moving. The level, the stop under the low, the shares from your risk. Then when it trades through, you just hit buy. If you're doing math while it's running, you'll chase it or size it wrong. And if the honest stop doesn't fit your risk, you skip it tonight, not in the middle of the move.
questions.lesson_line: Plan it before the open. The market order just runs the plan.
questions.simple: True. Plan it at night, so in the moment you only have to press buy.

reasons: stop first, size from the stop is the owner's rule A3
fixed before

questions.q: When a U&R fails, it most often closes back under the level first, then loses the undercut low.
questions.why: True. That's how it goes wrong most of the time. The reclaim doesn't hold, it closes back under the level, and then the undercut low gives way. It happens most when the index is breaking down too. That first close back under is your warning. The stop under the undercut low is your exit. And a loss there is the plan working.
questions.lesson_line: A failed U&R slips back under the level, then the low breaks.
questions.simple: True. It slips back under the level, then the undercut low breaks and the stop takes you out.

deeper.trap: A stop-out isn't proof the setup is broken. A loss at the stop is the plan working. Judge the setup over many trades, not by the last one.

reasons: one card line (c18)

questions.q: Stopped out, then it closed above your buy. How do you read that?
choices: A planned loss, wait for a trigger
Buy back now, it recovered
A mistake, the stop was too tight
Wait and buy the dip tomorrow morning
questions.answer: A planned loss, wait for a trigger
questions.why: A planned loss. It hit your stop, so you're out. That's the deal you made before the buy. The bounce stings, but it isn't a new trigger. If it sets up again, you take it as a new trade with its own stop. TRIP is the lesson here. It closed at 103.35 that day, then slid to 91.78 by August 1.
questions.lesson_line: The stop that shakes you out pays for the ones that keep falling.

wrong.Buy back now, it recovered: A bounce isn't a trigger. Buy again only on a new one, as a new trade.
wrong.A mistake, the stop was too tight: It sat 1.59% from the buy, right where I like it. A bounce after doesn't make it wrong.
wrong.Wait and buy the dip tomorrow morning: A dip isn't a trigger either. Let it set up again.

questions.story: Your stop at 100.56 filled when the stock dipped to 100.44. It then closed at 103.35, above your 102.18 entry.
questions.simple: A planned loss. A bounce isn't a trigger, so you wait for a new one.

deeper.counter: A stop-out followed by a bounce feels like proof the stop was wrong. TRIP dipped 12 cents through its stop and closed at 103.35. Twenty sessions after the buy it was at 94.03, and it hit 91.78 by 08-01.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (a new try needs a new trigger)

questions.q: What setup are you looking at here?
choices: An Oops reversal
A U&R of an older low
A Remount of the old low
A flat-base breakout
questions.why: An Oops. It opened under yesterday's close, traded under yesterday's low, and closed back over yesterday's close. All in one candle. The only level it undercut was yesterday's low. A U&R needs a level that matters more than that, like a low in the base, an average or a round number. Same idea, different name, and it has its own lesson.
questions.lesson_line: Only yesterday's low undercut means an Oops, not a U&R.

wrong.A U&R of an older low: No older low got touched. Yesterday's low alone makes it an Oops.
wrong.A Remount of the old low: A Remount comes after a long stay under a line. This was one day.
wrong.A flat-base breakout: Nothing broke out. It dipped and came back in one day.

questions.story: The reclaim day. The stock opened under its prior close and traded under yesterday's low. No other low or level was touched. It closed back over yesterday's close.
questions.simple: An Oops. The only thing it undercut was yesterday's low, so you judge it on one candle.

deeper.trap: The first half looks like a U&R, a dip under a low and a fast reclaim. The test is which level broke. Make it a prior high or a round number and the same candle becomes a U&R.

reasons: which levels count for a U&R is held with the owner, D-103
fixed before

questions.q: Which setup owns this?
choices: A Remount, bought on the retake
A U&R, it reclaimed
An Oops, it undercut a low
Gap Support
questions.answer: A Remount, bought on the retake
questions.why: A Remount. 5 or more closes under the line is a Remount. FDX closed under its level 8 times before the retake.
questions.lesson_line: Eight closes under a line is a Remount, not a U&R.

wrong.A U&R, it reclaimed: Up to 3 closes under is a U&R. Eight is a long stay, so the Remount card applies.
wrong.An Oops, it undercut a low: An Oops is one day of an undercut and reclaim. This stay was far longer.
wrong.Gap Support: Gap Support needs the gap-up day's low as the level. Nothing here says a gap.

questions.story: A leader closed under its 211.18 level for eight sessions in a row. Then it closed back above the line.

questions.q: Name the level first. Which one did this dip undercut?
choices: The gap-up day's low
A swing low in a base
A rising 20 EMA
A round number
questions.why: The gap-up day's low. Always name the level first, because it tells you what you're trading. A big earnings gap on 3x volume leaves a low everyone watches. Dipping under it shakes out the people who bought the gap. Closing back over it the same day traps the sellers. That works as a U&R, and an open gap like this also has its own lesson, Gap Support.
questions.lesson_line: Name the level first. A gap-up day's low is an obvious one.

wrong.A swing low in a base: There's no base here. The dip went under the gap-up day's low.
wrong.A round number: No round number in play. It's the gap-up day's low.
wrong.A rising 20 EMA: The story doesn't put an average there. The level is the gap-up day's low.

questions.story: A stock gapped up 9% on earnings, on 3x its usual volume. The gap is still open. Two weeks later it dips under the gap-up day's low and closes back above it that day.
questions.simple: The gap-up day's low. A big earnings gap leaves a low everyone watches.

deeper.trap: It looks like a plain swing-low U&R because the shape is the same. Name the level first. A still-open gap on heavy volume also has its own lesson, Gap Support.

reasons: one card line (c26)
which levels count for a U&R is held with the owner, D-103
fixed before

questions.q: What are you looking at on this chart?
choices: A U&R of the 20 EMA
A 2B of a swing low
An Oops at the prior close
A spring off a range floor
questions.why: A U&R of the 20 EMA. The leader closed over its rising 20 EMA, dipped under it during the day, and closed right back over. The average is the level. It didn't open under yesterday's close, so it's not an Oops. There's no swing low or flat range in play either. Look at the candle: a hammer, a long tail under the line and a close near the high. That's the U&R in one bar.
questions.lesson_line: Name the level. A rising average makes a good U&R.

wrong.A 2B of a swing low: No swing low got broken. The line it undercut is the 20 EMA.
wrong.An Oops at the prior close: An Oops opens under the prior close. This one didn't.
wrong.A spring off a range floor: There's no flat range here. The level is a rising average.

questions.story: The reclaim day. A leader closed above its rising 20 EMA yesterday. Today it dipped under the line and closed back above it.
questions.simple: A U&R with the rising 20 EMA as the level. It dipped under the line and closed back over.

deeper.counter: Put a prior swing low there instead and the same candles are still a U&R, since any obvious level works. Open it under the prior close and reclaim that close, and it's an Oops. The level and the candle set the name.

reasons: which levels count for a U&R is held with the owner, D-103
fixed before

questions.q: What do you call this setup?
choices: A spring below the floor
A U&R of a rising average
An Oops at the prior close
A Remount of the range floor
questions.why: A spring. The stock sat in a flat range for weeks with a floor it kept defending. It broke that floor, and the next day it was back inside. Wyckoff called that a spring, a quick break of the range's support that reverses right back in. Same trap idea as a U&R. The level just happens to be a range floor.
questions.lesson_line: Flat range, floor broken, back inside fast: that's a spring.

wrong.A U&R of a rising average: No average here. The level is the floor of a flat range.
wrong.An Oops at the prior close: An Oops is one candle off yesterday's close. This came after a long flat range.
wrong.A Remount of the range floor: A Remount comes after a long stay under the line. This was back the next day.

questions.story: A stock sat in a flat range for 20 sessions and touched the floor three times. It broke the floor and closed back inside the next day.
questions.simple: A spring. It broke the floor of a flat range and was back inside the next day.

deeper.trap: A spring and a U&R both break a level and take it back, so they feel alike. A spring needs a sideways range with a floor. Without one, the same candles may be a U&R or an Oops.

reasons: which levels count for a U&R is held with the owner, D-103
fixed before

questions.q: Buy the close?
choices: Pass; over 4% above the level
Buy; the close is strong and high
Buy half size and stay small
Buy with a stop under the close
questions.why: Pass. At the buy, price is no more than 4% over the level, and the close of 106.20 is more than 4% over the 100.00 level. We never buy more than 4% above the buy point. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the undercut low, so the distance grows and the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: The buy point is the level. Miss it, and let it go.

wrong.Buy; the close is strong and high: Strength is not the issue. The close sits well over the level, and we never chase past 4%.
wrong.Buy half size and stay small: Half size does not change the 4% line. We never buy more than 4% above the buy point.
wrong.Buy with a stop under the close: The stop belongs a few cents under the undercut low. A stop under the close is not the trade.

questions.story: A leader reclaims its 100.00 level and runs to a close at 106.20. You did not buy earlier. The undercut low is 98.40.
questions.simple: Pass, because the close of 106.20 is more than 4% over the 100.00 level, and we never chase past 4%.

deeper.trap: The buy point is the level, not the close. After a big reclaim day the close can sit well over 4% from the level, yet the stop still belongs under the undercut low. The distance grows, so the shares shrink, and the trade stops fitting.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (never chase past 4%)
the key needs arithmetic on the story's numbers

questions.q: The U&R is a good setup because it rarely touches the stop.
questions.why: False. Most of them touch the stop at some point. In our scan, 84.6% of hits did within 60 sessions, most after already making 1R or more. Yet 50.2% reached 3R before the stop. The edge isn't avoiding stops. It's small losses and a few big runners. So take the stop when it comes, and let the winners pay for it.
questions.lesson_line: Most U&Rs touch the stop. The winners pay for all of it.
questions.simple: False. Most touch the stop at some point, and the edge is small losses and a few big winners.

deeper.trap: 50.2% reaching 3R sounds like a high win rate, yet 84.6% also touched the stop. Both are true. One counts a trip to 3R before the stop. The other counts any touch of the stop in the 60 sessions.

reasons: scan numbers change when the scan is rerun
fixed before

questions.q: It's back over the level today. Can you take it?
choices: Skip it, the stop is too wide
Take full size, it reclaimed
Move the stop in to 3% and size up
Buy the close, it's a leader
questions.answer: Skip it, the stop is too wide
questions.why: Skip it. The stop belongs under 152.00, the low of the dip, and that's 8.08% from the buy. We take up to 5%, and I'd rather be at 1-3%. Past 5%, we wait for a tighter trigger. You can't fix it by pulling the stop in to 3% either. That puts it in the noise, not where the idea is wrong.
questions.lesson_line: Too wide a stop: skip it and wait for a tighter one.

wrong.Move the stop in to 3% and size up: Never move the stop to fit the size. A stop inside the noise is just a loss waiting.
wrong.Take full size, it reclaimed: The reclaim's fine. The stop isn't. The size comes from the stop, and this one's too far.
wrong.Buy the close, it's a leader: We don't buy closes. And being a leader doesn't shrink an 8.08% stop.

questions.story: The reclaim day. It closed under the 163.23 level two days running, then closed back above today. The lowest low was 152.00, 6.88% under the level. The stop would sit 8.08% below the buy.
questions.simple: Skip it. An 8.08% stop is way past the 5% we accept, so wait for a tighter trigger.

deeper.trap: The reclaim looked clean, which makes it tempting. The plan checks the stop first. A 6.88% dip is deep for this setup too, but the 8.08% stop settles it on its own.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (the stop distance)

questions.q: Which entry fits our stop rule?
choices: The level entry; the close is wide
The close entry; it is confirmed
Both fit; the level is the same one
Neither; wait a day for a retest
questions.answer: The level entry; the close is wide
questions.why: The level entry. A stop 3% or less from the buy is an A plus cue, and a stop over about 3% means size down or skip. The level entry has a 1.8% stop. The close entry has a 6.9% stop, far over the line.
questions.lesson_line: The entry near the level keeps the stop small. The late close does not.

wrong.The close entry; it is confirmed: Confirmed or not, 6.9% is far past about 3%. Size down or skip.
wrong.Both fit; the level is the same one: The level is the same, but the stop distance is not. The buy price moves the stop width.
wrong.Neither; wait a day for a retest: The level entry already fits, with a stop of 1.8%.

questions.story: Same U&R, two entries. Buy the reclaim at the level with a 1.8% stop, or buy the close of the day with a 6.9% stop.
questions.simple: The level entry fits, because its 1.8% stop is within about 3%, while the close entry's 6.9% stop is far past it.

deeper.trap: Same level, same undercut low, two buys. The stop stays under the undercut low, so buying higher only stretches the distance. That is why the late close breaks the size and the level entry does not.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (the stop distance)
grading cues conflict with E50 (see owner flags)

questions.q: Earnings are five sessions out. How do you handle it?
choices: Take it, sell before the report
Pass, the report is too close
Take it and hold through the report
Wait until the report has passed
questions.answer: Take it, sell before the report
questions.why: Take it, and plan to be out before the report. Our line is no new buys in the 3 days before earnings, and five sessions out clears it. But you don't hold a fresh trade through a report unless it's already up 5R. A report can gap a stock right through your stop. So mark the date, and be out before it unless the trade has paid you.
questions.lesson_line: Three days before earnings is the wall. Hold through only if up 5R.

wrong.Take it and hold through the report: Only a trade already up 5R holds through earnings.
wrong.Wait until the report has passed: You'd miss a good trigger for no reason. Five sessions is outside the window.
wrong.Pass, the report is too close: The no-buy window is the 3 days before a report. Five sessions out is fine.

questions.story: A clean U&R triggers. The next earnings report is five sessions away. Nothing else is pending.
questions.simple: Take it, but be out before the report unless it's up 5R. A gap can jump your stop.

deeper.trap: Two lines, not one. A report inside 3 days is a hard no for a new buy. Further out is fine, but a trade held into the report must already be up 5R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (the 3-day report wall and the 5R hold)

questions.q: How do you file this trade?
choices: A planned loss; the system worked
A mistake; the entry was early
A reason to widen stops next time
A sign to drop the setup
questions.answer: A planned loss; the system worked
questions.why: A planned loss. NVDA reached 0.67R, then was stopped on day 2. A reclaim that closes in its top half still gets stopped sometimes.
questions.lesson_line: Rules followed, stop hit: a planned loss. Next trade.

wrong.A mistake; the entry was early: The entry followed every rule. The stop is the exit, and this was a loss taken at it.
wrong.A reason to widen stops next time: The stop only moves up, never wider. A wider stop would only have made the loss bigger.
wrong.A sign to drop the setup: One stop says nothing. The edge is in the winners over many trades.

questions.story: You bought a U&R at 87.63 with the stop at 85.83. The reclaim day closed in its top half. Two sessions later the stock trades 83.02 and you are stopped.

questions.q: You took the loss. What's the lesson here?
choices: Stop worked, index hadn't turned
Should have added on the gap
One loss proves the U&R doesn't work
The index doesn't matter for a U&R
questions.why: The stop did its job, and the market hadn't turned. ADBE gapped up the next morning, then sold off all day through the stop. SPY made a lower low days later. That's the setting where U&Rs fail. The best ones come as the market turns up after a correction. So check the index before you trust the trap.
questions.lesson_line: A clean U&R means little while the index is still falling.

wrong.Should have added on the gap: It opened at 229.90 and closed at 213.80. An add at the open loses more.
wrong.One loss proves the U&R doesn't work: One stop proves nothing. Judge it over many trades.
wrong.The index doesn't matter for a U&R: It matters a lot. The best U&Rs come as the market turns up.

questions.story: You bought a U&R at the open, 218.83, with the stop at 214.73. The next morning it gapped up, sold off all day and closed at 213.80, through the stop. Days later the index made a lower low.
questions.simple: The stop did its job. The market hadn't turned yet, and that's when these fail.

deeper.trap: The gap up the next morning felt like proof. It sold off all day and closed at 213.80, through the 214.73 stop. A gap up isn't a turn in the index. The low of the move came on 04-02, the day SPY made a lower low.

reasons: rests on the owner's stop rule A4

questions.q: Buy again?
choices: No; a new try needs a new trigger
Yes, it is the same setup again
No; a stopped stock is off the list
Yes, at double size to win it back
questions.answer: No; a new try needs a new trigger
questions.why: No. After a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule. The stock being back near the old price is not a trigger. AMD's stop at 102.58 did its job: the next low was 99.51 on 09-20.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out is not a signal to buy again. Wait for a new trigger.

wrong.Yes, at double size to win it back: Size comes from the stop, not from the urge to win it back. Doubling makes a small loss bigger.
wrong.Yes, it is the same setup again: The same setup is not a trigger. A new try is a new trade with its own trigger and stop.
wrong.No; a stopped stock is off the list: A stop-out does not ban the stock. A new trigger makes it a new trade, up to 3 tries a week and 6 a month.

questions.story: You bought a U&R at 105.52 and were stopped at 102.58. Weeks later the stock is back near 105. Nothing new has triggered.
questions.simple: No, because buying again needs a new trigger, and the stock being back near your old buy is not one.

deeper.trap: Price back near your old entry feels like a second chance, but price is not a trigger. A new try also counts toward the cap of 3 tries a week and 6 a month on one stock.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (a new try needs a new trigger)

questions.q: Do you buy that open?
choices: Yes, it's back over, within 4%
No, wait for a close back above it
No, a gap means you skip it
Only if the volume doubles
questions.why: Yes. It opened back over the level, so the open is your trigger. 159.97 is only 0.4% over 159.37, nowhere near our 4% chase line. Two closes under is still a fast retake, and how fast is a judgment. Market order at the open, stop a few cents under the low of the dip. WYNN was the slowest of our ten winners to 3R, 8 days, and still ran 26.0R.
questions.lesson_line: A gap back over the level is the reclaim. Buy the open.

wrong.No, wait for a close back above it: We buy the trigger, never the close. Here the open itself is the trade back over.
wrong.No, a gap means you skip it: A gap back over the level is fine when it's this close. 0.4% is nothing.
wrong.Only if the volume doubles: Volume raises the grade. It's not a must for the buy.

questions.story: The level is 159.37, and it has closed under it two days running. Tomorrow it opens at 159.97.
questions.simple: Yes. It opened back over the level and only a little above it, so the open is the trigger.

deeper.example: WYNN, 2013-11-21. The level was 159.37 and it closed under it twice. Then it gapped back over, and the buy was the open, 159.97. The stop was 157.43, 1.59% away. Slowest of the ten to 3R at 8 days, and it still ran to 26.0R.

reasons: the 3-session window is the card's proposed line (D-036)
the entry trigger style waits on D-003
rests on the owner's rulebook (the 4% limit)

questions.q: Reclaim day: it dipped under the level and closed back above. Check the 50-day. Do you take it?
choices: Take it, the 50-day is rising
Pass, the 50-day is falling
Pass, the undercut is too small
Wait, buy only on a second close
questions.why: Take it. Look at the setup. A two-week shelf sits on a rising 50-day. One poke under the level, then a reclaim that closed near the high. That's a leader resting, not breaking. NTAP was bought at 23.05 with the stop at 22.67, 1.65% away. It ran 31.4R. A shallow dip like this is what you want.
questions.lesson_line: Rising 50-day, shallow dip, quick reclaim. That's the trade.

wrong.Pass, the 50-day is falling: Look again. The 50-day runs up under the whole shelf.
wrong.Pass, the undercut is too small: Shallow is good. In our scan, undercuts within 3% did better than deeper ones.
wrong.Wait, buy only on a second close: The trigger is the trade back over the level. NTAP's buy was 23.05, a cent over 23.04.

questions.simple: Take it. The 50-day is rising, and the dip was shallow and taken right back.

deeper.counter: Put the same candles over a falling 50-day and I'd pass. Check the average first, then the candles.

reasons: scan numbers change when the scan is rerun
the rising 50-day check is a proposed card line

questions.q: Reclaim day: a level got undercut and taken back the same day. Now check the 200-day. What's your call?
choices: Pass, it's under a falling 200-day
Pass, the reclaim took too long
Take it, it's over a rising 200-day
Take it, it reclaimed the same day
questions.why: Pass. The close was 9.7% under a falling 200-day. For a stock, under the 200-day is a hard no, however clean the candle is. The only exceptions are indexes and levered ETFs, on a reversal extension or a parabolic long. MSFT's a stock. Put it on watch and let it get back over the line first.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day, a stock's U&R is a watch, not a buy.

wrong.Take it, it reclaimed the same day: A same-day reclaim doesn't override the 200-day. It closed 9.7% under it.
wrong.Take it, it's over a rising 200-day: Look again. It's 9.7% under the line, and the line's falling.
wrong.Pass, the reclaim took too long: It came back the same day. The reason to pass is the 200-day.

questions.simple: Pass. A stock under its 200-day is a hard no, however clean the shape is.

deeper.trap: The shape is perfect, a level undercut and taken back the same day, so it feels like a buy. The 200-day check comes before the candle check.

reasons: no longs under the 200-day is the owner's rule B26
which 200-day exceptions apply is held with the owner, D-009

questions.q: Friday brings a fourth trigger on the same stock. Do you take it?
choices: No, three tries a week is the cap
Yes, it's a new trigger
Yes, if you cut the size in half
No, it's off limits for the whole month
questions.answer: No, three tries a week is the cap
questions.why: No. Three tries a week on one stock is the cap, and Monday to Wednesday used all three. A new trigger is needed, but it isn't enough on its own. Three stops in three days means the stock isn't working right now, or you're forcing it. Step away. You get 6 tries a month, so it can come back next week.
questions.lesson_line: Three tries a week on one stock. Then you walk away.

wrong.Yes, if you cut the size in half: Half size is still a try, and the cap is used up.
wrong.Yes, it's a new trigger: A new trigger is needed, but the cap still applies. Three tries a week.
wrong.No, it's off limits for the whole month: Not the month. The cap is 3 a week and 6 a month, and you've used 3.

questions.story: You were stopped out of this stock on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, each time on its own fresh trigger. A fourth U&R trigger appears on Friday.
questions.simple: No. Three tries a week on one stock is the cap, so walk away and look again next week.

deeper.trap: A new trigger is necessary but not enough. The cap is a second gate, so a clean trigger still waits when the week's 3 tries are used.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (the try limits)

questions.q: Your account is 100,000 and you're risking 0.25% on this one. How many shares do you buy?
questions.why: 38 shares. 0.25% of 100,000 is $250 at risk. 242.18 minus 235.64 is 6.54 a share. 250 over 6.54 is 38.23, so round down to 38. Always round down, or you risk more than you planned. The stop is 2.70% away, inside the 1-3% I like. The 40% position cap isn't close, so the stop sets the size.
questions.lesson_line: The size comes from the stop. Always round down.
questions.simple: 38 shares. Divide the dollars at risk by the risk a share, then round down.

deeper.example: LULU: bought at 242.18 with the stop at 235.64. It made 1.26R, then was stopped three sessions later as the market broke down. The size came from the stop, so the loss stayed the one planned.

questions.q: You wrote your stop in your journal before the open. That counts as a real stop.
questions.why: False. A stop is an order sitting with your broker. A line in your journal can't sell anything. If the stock drops while you're away from the screen, the order fills and the journal doesn't. Put the stop in with the broker the moment you buy, and only ever move it up.
questions.lesson_line: A stop is an order with the broker, not a line in a notebook.
questions.simple: False. Only a real order with the broker gets you out, and a journal note can't sell anything.

reasons: real broker stop is the owner's rule D41

questions.q: When does that stop order actually go in?
questions.story: You buy the reclaim at 109.63. The undercut low is 108.30. You plan to place the stop order after lunch, once the market settles.
choices: Now, with the broker, as you buy
After lunch, once it settles
Only if it nears the undercut low
Never, the undercut low is the stop
questions.answer: Now, with the broker, as you buy
questions.why: Now, the moment you buy. The stop sits a few cents under the undercut low, here 108.25, five cents under 108.30. A morning flush doesn't wait for your lunch break. If it drops through that low before noon, you want to already be out, not watching it. A stop only protects you while the order is in.
questions.lesson_line: The stop goes in with the buy, not after lunch.

wrong.Never, the undercut low is the stop: The low is just a price on the chart. The stop is a real order a few cents under it.
wrong.After lunch, once it settles: A morning flush finds you with no stop at all. The order goes in with the buy.
wrong.Only if it nears the undercut low: By then it can flush right through. The order's in from the start.

questions.simple: Now, as you buy. A stop only protects you once the order is in.

deeper.trap: After lunch sounds harmless while the stock sits above the stop. But a flush before then finds you with no order on the book. A stop only protects the hours it's in.

reasons: real broker stop is the owner's rule D41
